extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction and criticism (literary magazine audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts of short fiction and a critical essay discussing qualities of a novelist's style and technique; aimed at evaluating what makes literary writing authentic, vital, or deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: explicitness_vs_tacit_implication
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gertrude hated for anything to be latent or tacit or implicit: if there was an inexpressible secret to the world — or one unexpressed because taken for granted by everybody — she would express it or die.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing insistently explicit revelation: the writer forces hidden or tacit aspects of life into explicit statement. The essay warns this can become an aesthetic principle (express everything) and may overdetermine meaning; use explicitness intentionally, mindful of subtlety lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: analysis_that_dissects_to_murder
rubrics_metrics.description: “Her books... did not murder to dissect, but dissected to murder.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopic, purely analytical treatment of characters or phenomena can 'kill' their humanity. Accurate, clinical analysis that treats people as specimens risks destroying emotional life and reader sympathy; maintain humane engagement even when analyzing.

rubrics_metrics.name: knowledge_of_being_human
rubrics_metrics.description: “She did not know — or rather, did not believe — what it was like to be a human being.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard for authentic writing: the author must be able to inhabit and convey the lived experience of human beings. Lack of this empathy/knowledge produces inauthentic, detached work; cultivate an interior sense of characters' humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance_microscopic_detail_with_sweep_and_sex
rubrics_metrics.description: “If Gertrude had had sweep and sex (her method was microscopic, her sex statistical) she might have been considered a Great American Novelist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical precision and microscopic method are valuable but insufficient. Good novels often combine detailed observation with narrative sweep, vitality, and erotic or emotional energy; aim for both scope and detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_explaining_everything_by_worst_motives
rubrics_metrics.description: “She saw the worst: it was, indeed, her only principle of explanation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the 'worst' motive as a default explanatory principle makes interpretation cynical and reductive. Writers should avoid flattening characters' motives to a single negative explanation; allow complexity and mixed motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: technical_accuracy_without_vitality_is_inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best of Gertrude's books were habitat groups in a Museum of Natural History: topography, correct; meteorological information, correct; condition of skins, good; mounting of horns, correct... And yet... the animals moved, a little stiffly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate, well-researched detail (topography, locale, facts) is necessary but not sufficient; such correctness can produce lifeless, museum-like writing unless animated by feeling, movement, and living characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: recognize_and_write_human_generosity_and_tenderness
rubrics_metrics.description: “To her generosity, tenderness, good-humored indifference were unaccountable except as fear or caution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for humane fiction: acknowledge virtues like generosity and tenderness as real human forces, not merely symptoms of fear. Representing these qualities grounds characters and creates moral nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: style_must_not_block_truth_or_humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gertrude had a style in which you couldn't tell the truth if you tried — and when, except when it was a shameful one, had Gertrude ever tried?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style should enable truthful, humane expression. Excessive mannerisms or theoretical postures can obstruct the communication of genuine feeling or truth; prioritize clarity and moral honesty over mannered effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: private_life_should_inform_public_work
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sidney kept Gertrude alive: without him she would have gone on functioning drearily, striking at anything that came in reach, but she would hardly have lived; yet Sidney, and the part of Gertrude that lived because of Sidney, never got into Gertrude’s books at all — she would have been ashamed and embarrassed to see them there.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic values how a writer’s private life energizes their work; excluding the private self from art can render it thin. Consider letting genuine private affections and dependencies inform character and emotional texture (without forced confession).

rubrics_metrics.name: authentic_representation_of_children
rubrics_metrics.description: “This was what Gertrude didn't like about children: they didn't act like grown-ups.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing children, avoid projecting adult logic or affect onto them. Children should be portrayed according to their own perceptions and behaviors; respect their distinctiveness to avoid flattening or condescending portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_cruel_moralizing_against_the_exceptional
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you were one of the ordinary lumps... you were safe from her; but if you moved or spoke, were for some reason, from the beginning, extraordinary, she slapped you in the face...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of a destructive critical stance: do not punish or mock characters (or writers) simply for being exceptional or alive. Excessive moralizing or public shaming within prose can alienate readers and harm dimensional characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: prioritize_roots_over_surface_convention
rubrics_metrics.description: “Grammar and capital letters are conventions, the last twigs on the tree of life; it was the roots that Gertrude sawed patiently away at.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic acknowledges that surface grammatical conventions are subordinate to deeper thematic or moral concerns. Still, this should be balanced: breaking rules for root-level insight can be powerful, but avoid mistaking rule-breaking for depth itself.
